title-group.article-title: Pricing and Coordination of a Dual-Channel Supply Chain Considering Price Reference Effect and Return Service

abstract.p: With the development of dual-channel supply chains, consumers have more purchasing options, and reference price effects have become increasingly important in shaping their purchasing decisions. To attract consumers, some suppliers and retailers need to adjust their pricing strategies and provide measures such as return services to gain more profits. To address these problems, considering that the reference price effect and return service level are important factors affecting the supply chain, we construct game-theoretic models for a manufacturer-dominated dual-channel supply chain comprising one manufacturer and one retailer, use them to examine the optimal decisions, and analyze the effects of the reference price effect and return service level on the supply chain. Then, a two-part pricing contract is developed. The results show that, within the feasible parameter region, a higher return service level improves the total supply chain profit. In the parameter regions examined, a stronger reference price effect increases the manufacturer’s online channel demand and revenue, whereas the retailer’s offline channel demand and revenue tend to decrease when the return service level is relatively low. Furthermore, the manufacturer’s profit increases, while the retailer’s profit may decline at relatively low return service levels. A sufficiently high return service level can mitigate this adverse effect. The proposed two-part pricing contract yields a feasible interval of fixed transfer fees within which the profit conflict between the manufacturer and the retailer can be resolved.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Dual-channel supply chains have grown rapidly in recent years with the fast-paced development of information technology and e-commerce. Many manufacturers such as Apple Store and Huawei Mall now open online channels alongside offline retailers, selling products through their official websites, online flagship stores, and physical stores simultaneously [1,2]. The dual-channel model enables manufacturers to expand market coverage and increase profits, but it also intensifies conflicts of interest between channels and complicates pricing decisions of channel managers, hindering the healthy development of the supply chain. If the online selling price is too high relative to the offline retail price, consumers may perceive an unfavorable price difference and become reluctant to purchase. Conversely, an excessively low online selling price may erode the retailer’s profit and intensify channel conflicts. Meanwhile, as consumers pay more attention to service experience, product returns have become a non-negligible problem in online retailing [3,4]. A higher return service level directly increases channel demand and also raises the consumer reference price, thereby influencing demand allocation and profits across channels [5,6]. Therefore, manufacturers need to continuously adjust their pricing and return service strategies to adapt to market changes.

Given the critical role of pricing in a dual-channel supply chain, substantial scholarly attention has been devoted to this area. Previous studies have extensively examined the reference price effect in dynamic pricing and inventory management [7,8,9] and the return service in pricing and coordination [10,11]. However, these two factors are largely examined in isolation, and the existing models cannot explain how a firm should determine prices given the return service level, and how the return service level affects equilibrium outcomes, when the two effects interact. To address this gap, we aim to investigate the pricing and coordination decisions of a manufacturer-dominated dual-channel supply chain considering both the reference price effect and the return service level. Specifically, we develop a dual-channel pricing model in which a manufacturer sells directly online and wholesales to a retailer selling offline, and then we examine the decentralized and centralized pricing scenarios and design a two-part pricing contract to coordinate the decentralized chain. The main contributions are as follows: (1) we incorporate the reference price effect and the return service level in a unified framework and reveal a channel-conflict dilemma that the existing models cannot capture; (2) we derive the parameter conditions under which the equilibrium is unique and characterize the feasible interval of the fixed transfer fee ensuring coordination and individual rationality; (3) we numerically quantify the impacts of the two factors on the equilibrium outcomes. The findings provide a theoretical foundation and an actionable reference for manufacturers and retailers’ pricing and return service strategies in the examined dual-channel setting.

The structure of the paper is arranged as follows: Section 2 reviews the related literature. Section 3 constructs some basic models of supply chain considering online returns and return service and discuss their decisions and effects, and develops a two-part pricing coordination mechanism and conducts the corresponding analysis. Section 4 provides a numerical example and analysis. Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines the prospects for future research.

sec.title: 2. Literature Review
sec.p: The diversification of shopping methods has offered customers more options, prompting numerous manufacturers to embrace the dual-channel supply chain model. This, in turn, has facilitated the emergence and growth of dual-channel supply chains while heightening competition between manufacturers and retailers. Considering that the influence of reference price and level of return service stand as core factors impacting the profitability of supply chain merchants, a growing number of scholars are engaging in research on the pricing of dual-channel supply chains from these two aspects. Through a systematic review of the relevant literature, it emerges that existing research is committed to finding out how these two aspects affect supply chain pricing decisions and coordination.

sec.title: 2.1. Reference Price Effect
sec.p: In recent years, research into the implications of reference pricing has witnessed significant expansion, a development that aligns with the rapid proliferation of e-commerce. Researchers have concentrated on three areas: the determinants of reference prices, the consequences of the reference price influence, and their practical applications. Mazumdar et al. [12] discovered that a variety of factors impact reference pricing, including past purchasing experiences, price susceptibility, brand commitment, product quality, and promotional campaigns. Nasiry et al. [13] also advocated that consumer reference prices should be calculated by taking the weighted mean of the minimum and latest purchase prices. In relation to the previous work, Zhang et al. [7] claimed that consumer reference prices draw on historical prices, with updates informed by contemporary market prices and memory-related variables. The findings revealed that a stronger memory factor corresponds to a greater weight assigned to short-term prices, suggesting that consumers are more susceptible to current pricing and exhibit weaker loyalty to the product. Wang [14] explored the dynamic pricing dilemma that enterprises face when customers’ reference prices change over time. The effects of reference pricing can also exert an influence on inventory levels, price promotions, advertising levels, and earnings, among other things. Lin [15] investigated the way manufacturers’ proposals of zero prices influence pricing strategies within supply chains from the viewpoint of supply chain participants under risk aversion conditions. The findings indicated that the maximum reference price strategy, along with the minimum reference price strategy, serves to boost manufacturers’ profitability. A reference price creation model was created by Fibich et al. [16] to study how asymmetric reference prices affect the profitability of price promotion campaigns. Malekian et al. [17] examined the ways in which reference price effects shape manufacturers’ promotional pricing and advertising decisions in a dual-channel supply chain composed of a single manufacturer and its exclusive downstream retailer. Yang et al. [18] also derived the optimal retail price and service level in a dual-channel supply chain with reference price effects. The relationship between the reference inventory level and the target reference price, as well as the linkage between the benchmark inventory level and the reference inventory level when they occur concurrently, was examined by Chen et al. [9] Chen et al. [19] further investigated dynamic pricing in the presence of reference price effects and consumer strategic behavior, showing that consumers’ strategic waiting may erode the gains from the reference price effect.

Furthermore, a wide range of dynamic pricing choices, including those involving cooperative innovation, advertising and promotion, inventory management, and optimal pricing, are impacted by the reference price effect. In their analysis, Zhang et al. [20] conducted an investigation into the reference price impact and saturation level within the dynamic pricing framework for durable goods and found that market saturation level, alongside reference price effects of customers, influenced pricing strategy. Sun et al. [21] studied pricing policies in dual distribution channels and showed that the reference effect of official prices significantly reshapes the equilibrium price structure. In a two-period market scenario, Wu [22] examined how retailers’ dynamic pricing and inventory decisions are affected by reference prices and provided appropriate optimization solutions. Zhao et al. [23] analyzed information-technology-driven operational decisions in a supply chain with random demand disruption and reference effects, and Zhao et al. [24] examined price decisions with asymmetric reference effects and information sharing in dual-channel supply chains. Panda and Maiti [25] developed two-period decision strategies in a dual-channel supply chain considering reference prices and online reviews, while Dai et al. [26] extended the reference price effect to dual-channel re-manufacturing supply chains under static and dynamic games. Wang et al. [27] studied process improvement under the reference price effect, and Huang et al. [28] incorporated the reference price effect into emission reduction and pricing decisions under carbon-emission policy. In a perishable product inventory model, Dye and Yang [8] established reference prices and invested and priced them.

sec.title: 2.2. Return Service
sec.p: As an important part of customers’ consumption experience, the return service is attracting more and more scholars’ attention. Many scholars at home and abroad have conducted detailed studies and found that a return service has a huge impact on pricing. Ofek et al. [3] included customer returns and retail services in the customer utility function to study the pricing of both channels under the risk of returns. A key result showed that when retailer competition is minimal, online channels may boost in-store staffing while reducing profitability. Chen and Bell [4] investigated how consumer product returns influence the pricing strategies of manufacturers and retailers, as well as the revenue generated from three channel structures, MS, VN and RS, respectively. Ren et al. [5] studied pricing strategies adopted by manufacturers and retailers across various channel structures. Ren et al. [6] examined how competition affects return pricing and optimal pricing in an internet environment. They created a novel agreement to align the two-path supply chain, ensuring mutual benefits for both retailers and manufacturers. Wang et al. [29] derived the optimal operational policies of a dual-channel supply chain considering return service and showed that the return service level significantly affects equilibrium decisions. Based on consumer utility, Fan [30] investigated how the online return rate influences goods pricing under different channel models. Results showed that an increased return rate in the network channel is prone to leading to higher pricing for the said channel, with a corresponding decrease regarding the brand supplier’s profit. Xu et al. [31] analyzed pricing and sales-effort decisions in a dual-channel supply chain with channel preference, cross-channel return, and free-riding behavior under a revenue-sharing contract. Wang and He [32] investigated the optimal decisions of modularity, prices, and return policy in a dual-channel supply chain under mass customization, and Lin et al. [33] showed that providing return-freight insurance may do more harm than good to dual-channel e-commerce retailers under certain conditions.

In addition, return service affects both supply chain coordination and overall profits. Pasternack [34] proposed the “pricing and return” problem from the perishable category and realized a supply chain involving multiple retailers. Mukhopadhyay et al. [35] studied return behaviors in direct sales channels via the internet and investigated pricing decisions as well as return strategies in the supply chain. Ferguson et al. [10] explored the coordination of supply chains based on target recall contracts for defect-free returns to reduce return rates, improve retailer effort and increase supply chain revenue.

sec.title: 2.3. Pricing Decisions and Coordination
sec.p: The process of developing a price strategy for a product or a service and putting it into practice all the way through the supply chain is denoted as pricing choices in a supply chain. Achieving supply chain coordination and choosing appropriate pricing levels to balance profitability, market share, and customer choice are also necessary. Scholars have increasingly researched demand dynamics, cost structures, service quality, inventory management, information sharing, and consumer decision-making behaviors.

For pricing decisions, numerous influencing elements, including supply, demand, price, quality, inventory, information, and customer behavior, have different relationships. Built on the postulation of demand that is sensitive to service and price, Yan et al. [36] introduced a supply chain framework with a dual-channel approach where suppliers take the lead, examining optimal pricing strategies across three distinct scenarios: a traditional retail setting, a centrally coordinated dual-channel system, and a hierarchical master–slave game structure. Soleimani et al. [37] created a bi-directional distribution framework that takes demand disruption and production cost into account. They also examined the best pricing strategy when both factors were present as well as the best pricing strategy when both factors were absent. Beyond demand and production-cost disruptions, Hilger et al. [38] examined the resilience strategies of Ukrainian agribusinesses under prolonged wartime shocks. Their findings highlight the importance of dynamic capabilities, logistics adaptation, and stakeholder relationships in maintaining supply chain operations under extreme uncertainty. Wang et al. [39] delved into the challenge of determining the perfect pricing strategy when introducing advertising initiatives within a supply chain that operates through two distinct channels—namely, the manufacturer’s own direct sales platform and the more traditional brick-and-mortar retail outlets. The dual-channel supply chain pricing strategies under information symmetry were examined by Xiao et al. [40]. They developed two models, the Stackelberg and Bertrand game models, for cooperation between the electronic channels of manufacturers and the services of retailers. And then, they discovered that the prices of both channels under Bertrand competition were higher than those under Stackelberg competition. From an interorganizational perspective, Zhao et al. [41] investigated the contingent role of supply chain e-linkage in green supply chain practices and found that organizational support facilitates green practices, whereas digital linkages may generate both synergistic and antagonistic effects depending on the nature of interfirm relationships, highlighting the potential influence of power imbalances on supply chain cooperation. The supply chain choice problem was examined by Wang et al. [42] where the retailer’s level of risk aversion was full knowledge vs. private information. Fan et al. [43] proceeded from the assumption that consumers fall into distinct categories based on their openness to digital retail channels to investigate the pricing approach within a dual-channel supply network comprising one manufacturer and one retailer.

Furthermore, customers directly affect price decisions as the last link in a supply chain. Therefore, several academics have investigated how different customer preferences and behaviors affect supply chains. Dan et al. [2] investigated how manufacturers and retailers’ pricing decisions were impacted when they took consumer service loyalty into account within a dual-channel supply chain. Gu et al. [44] studied the pricing coordination of a dual-channel supply chain considering offline in-sale service, and showed that the in-sale service level significantly affects pricing and coordination decisions. The comparison of pricing decisions between dual-channel supply chains and a single traditional channel was investigated by Shen et al. [45]. Taleizadeh et al. [46] examined sustainability, pricing, and marketing decisions in a dual-channel supply chain with different retailing scenarios. Xu et al. [47] explored pricing and revenue tactics for dual-channel supply chains and developed a model of customer transfer behaviors based on consumer utility. Liu et al. [48] developed a pricing strategy for a dual-channel supply chain considering online reviews and in-sale service, and Phadnis and Fine [49] further analyzed market expansion through online buying to store pickup and its implications for end-to-end supply chain strategy. Bostan et al. [50] systematically reviewed the implications of AI adoption in last-mile delivery and indicated that AI-enabled logistics can improve operational efficiency while introducing workforce management challenges, underscoring the broader operational considerations associated with e-commerce channel development.

Designing cooperation contracts is essential to improving the effectiveness of dual-channel supply chain activities since channel conflicts happen. Scholars have mostly developed coordination mechanisms like cost-sharing, revenue sharing, price discounts, and two-part pricing in their studies of coordination strategies for dual-channel supply chains. A coordination framework was put forth by Kunter [51], wherein a retailer receives a commission from a producer and both parties split the cost of the market. The power industry’s supply chain coordination was examined by Oliveira et al. [52]. A combination contract based on inter-channel revenue sharing and inventory cost sharing was put up by Chiang [1] to create a two-channel supply chain synergy during uncertain demand periods. Boyaci [53] proposed a two-part compensating commission contract. When the offline inventory of the retailers and the internet-based inventory of the manufacturers can balance each other out, this can enhance the supply chain’s inventory level. As a result, the strategy can raise the supply chain’s overall revenue. Research by Chen et al. [54], Ryan et al. [55], and Xu et al. [56] suggests that revenue sharing agreements are a useful tool for fostering synergy in supply chains with several channels. Yan and Pei [57] investigated how a product’s network compatibility affected their advertising expense-sharing arrangement in a dual-channel supply chain context. Li et al. [58] further suggested an enhanced risk-sharing contract by examining the issue of supply chain cooperation in the context of demand-volatile markets, with the target of coordinating the supply chain’s primary topics. In Hu et al.’s [59] comparative analysis, the effects of three different contract types—wholesale pricing, incentive-penalty, profit-sharing, and franchise—on supply chain synergy were examined. The influence of demand disturbance on synergy contracts in dual-channel supply chains was analyzed by Cao et al. [60]. Li et al. [61] investigated the effect of retailer fairness preferences on low-carbon supply chain synergy in the presence of producer fairness preferences. Yu et al. [62] studied recycling, pricing decisions, and coordination in a dual-channel closed-loop supply chain from a dynamic perspective, extending coordination analysis to the circular-economy context.

Although the existing literature has extensively examined dual-channel pricing and coordination, there are significant differences in the main features considered across the studies. To clarify the positioning of the present study, Table 1 compares representative studies in terms of channel structure, return assumptions, reference-price formulation, decision variables, contract type, sustainability-related dimensions where applicable, and specific contribution.

Drawing on the above analysis, the extant studies of return services in dual-channel supply chains have emphasized pricing or competition, while few studies jointly examine the reference price effect and the return service level. In view of this, we develop dual-channel supply chain models incorporating the reference price effect and the return service level and examine their effects on optimal channel prices, channel demands, and the profits of individual supply chain members and the entire supply chain. We further propose a two-part pricing contract to resolve conflicts between the supply chain and its members.

sec.title: 3. Pricing and Coordination Considering Reference Price Effect and Return Service Level
sec.p: As information technology and e-commerce develop rapidly, there has been a significant shift in consumers’ consumption behaviors. They can utilize the internet to obtain commodity information quickly and easily and to compare prices and performance of similar goods across different channels. The existence of different pricing channels leads to reference prices for consumers. Although consumers can get product information and make comparisons via the internet, they are not able to have direct contact with the product, so they do not get the true value, and the gap between the value of the product itself and the consumer’s value expectation exacerbates the problem of returns. The reference price effect influences consumers’ purchasing decisions, and it also exerts notable influence on merchants’ pricing decisions. The level of return service affects consumers’ reference prices to a certain extent, which in turn affects consumers’ purchasing decisions along with merchants’ pricing decisions and profitability. It is thus crucial to explore how the dual-channel supply chain is affected by the reference price effect. To describe and analyze well the problem of decision-making with regards to a dual supply chain composed of a single retailer and a single manufacturer, considering the reference price and the level of return service, we develop some dual channel supply chain models to investigate the optimal pricing decision and the impact of the reference price effect and the level of return service on the pricing decision of the manufacturer and the retailer.

sec.title: 3.1. Some Assumptions

p.italic: Assume that there is a manufacturer-led dual-channel supply chain comprising one manufacturer and one retailer. Both parties are assumed to be risk-neutral and fully rational.

statement.p: In a manufacturer-dominated dual-channel supply chain, a manufacturer sells products directly to consumers on the internet at retailer price and wholesales them to retailers at wholesale price, and the retailer sells them to consumers at retailer price. Assume p1, p2 and ω represent online channel retail price, physical store retail price, and bulk wholesale price, respectively. Since both the manufacturer and the retailer provide return services to consumers, assume that e represent the return service level provided by the online channel and the offline channel, respectively, and e is treated as an exogenous parameter which satisfies 0 < e < 1. For analytical tractability, the two channels are assumed to provide a standardized return service level e, which represents a coordinated service standard for the same product.

Assume that the manufacturer and downstream retailer cooperate on only one product and the goods can only be purchased through these two channels, a represents the cross-price elasticity coefficient which satisfies a(0 < a < 1). D(D > 0) denotes the essential requirement of the market, d1 and d2 denote the demand of online and offline channels respectively, and v(0 < v < 1) denotes the degree of consumer preference for offline retail channels. t denotes the consumer’s reference price, b(0 < b ≤ 1) denotes the coefficient of influence generated by the reference price effect, b(t − p1) denotes the impact of the reference price effect on the demand of the online direct sales channel, and b(t − p2) denotes the impact of the reference price effect on the demand of the offline retail channel.

In supply chain management, both manufacturers and retailers that offer return services are susceptible to the influence of return service quality. Following the linear anchoring specification of reference prices widely used in the literature [12,13], the reference price is expressed as t = (1 − k)p1 + kp2 + ue, where k(0 < k < 1) indicates the degree to which offline retail prices influence the reference price and u(0 < u < 1) indicates the extent to which the return service level affects the reference price.

Assume e and u denote the return service level and the extent to which the return service level affects the reference price, respectively. Based on Chen and Bell [4] and others who found that the return service and the level of returns are positively correlated with market demand, it is assumed that r(0 < r < 1) denotes the demand–return rate and r is treated as an exogenous constant that is independent of the return service level. The cost incurred in providing services related to returns is assumed as: Ce=12ce2 where c(0 < c < 1) denotes the cost factor of providing returns services [2,3].

sec.title: 3.2. Some Basic Models
sec.p: In a two-channel supply chain influenced by reference price effects and return services, the demand corresponding to the manufacturer’s online channel and the retailer’s offline channel includes four factors, which are all affected by channel-related preference tendencies: base demand, commodity prices, reference price effects, and return services. Following the standard linear-demand specification in dual-channel pricing [2,4], the demand of each channel decreases in its own price and increases in the cross-channel price, the reference-price advantage, and the return service level. The direct service term captures consumers’ immediate utility from a more convenient return process, whereas the indirect term through the reference price captures the behavioral effect of perceived transaction value. These two channels represent distinct mechanisms and therefore are not treated as duplicate benefits. Therefore, the demand functions of manufacturers and retailers are described as below:(1)d1=1−vD−p1+ap2+bt−p1+θe(2)d2=vD−p2+ap1+bt−p2+θe

sec.title: 3.4. A Pricing Coordination Mechanism
sec.p: Based on the foregoing model analysis, the total profit of the dual-channel supply chain under decentralized decision-making is lower than that under centralized decision-making in the admissible parameter region. In reality, both manufacturers and retailers tend to prioritize maximizing their individual interests, making centralized decision-making challenging to implement. Therefore, emphasis should be placed on coordinating the decision-making of manufacturers and retailers within decentralized decision-making frameworks so that manufacturers and retailers can obtain more benefits. The return service tends to improve the gains of both the manufacturer and the retailer within the admissible parameter region, whereas the reference price impact is detrimental to the retailer’s profit when the return service level is not sufficiently high. Therefore, this chapter designs a two-part pricing contract to improve the profitability of the dual-channel supply chain as a whole. The dual-channel supply chain coordination problem influenced by return service and reference price effect is investigated.

Following the standard notion in the supply chain coordination literature, a contract is said to coordinate the supply chain if it induces the decentralized members to replicate the centralized decisions (prices and demands) and thereby enables the decentralized system to achieve the centralized total profit; the contract is individually rational if each member earns at least its decentralized profit. The sequence of events is as follows: (i) at the beginning of the game, the manufacturer offers the two-part pricing contract, consisting of a lower wholesale price and a fixed fee; (ii) the retailer accepts the contract only if its profit under the contract is not lower than its decentralized profit; (iii) after acceptance, the manufacturer commits to the centralized online price, while the retailer independently determines its offline retail price by maximizing its own profit given the contracted wholesale price. The wholesale price is set to induce the retailer’s offline price to coincide with the centralized optimum. Neither party can unilaterally revise the manufacturer’s committed online price or the contract terms after acceptance; (iv) after the sales are completed, the fixed fee is settled between the two parties.

The two-part pricing contract has a mechanism whereby the manufacturer wholesales the product to the retailer at a lower wholesale price wo. The manufacturer, as the dominant party, charges the retailer a fixed fee at the end of the sale F. Let π1o,π2o denote the profits of the manufacturer and retailer, respectively; their specific formulas are as follows:(34)π1o=1−rp1d1+wd2−12ce2+F(35)π2o=1−rp2d2−wd2−12ce2−F

sec.title: 4. Numerical Analysis
sec.p: Owing to the complexity of the game equilibrium solutions, we employ numerical simulations to examine how the reference price effect and the return service level affect the equilibrium outcomes under decentralized decision-making, centralized decision-making, and the two-part pricing coordination contract. The numerical analyses are performed in MATLAB R2024b. Because no direct empirical calibration is undertaken, we demonstrate the model’s implications with an illustrative baseline parameter set that satisfies theoretical feasibility conditions and reflects realistic operational characteristics of the dual-channel supply chain. The parameter settings and their roles in the analysis are summarized in Table 3. Throughout this section, color shading is used to aid visualization of the surfaces, and numerical values should be read from the axes. Where multiple surfaces are shown, their parameter setting or decision-making scenarios are identified by the surface labels.

sec.title: 4.1. Analysis of How Reference Price Effects and Return Services Impact Decisions Under Decentralized Decision-Making
sec.p: Let D=200,a=0.8,k=23,r=0.02,u=0.2,θ=0.8,c=0.5, and take v1 = 0.3, v2 = 0.8 for comparative analysis. We can plot the impact diagram illustrating how the reference price effect and return service level influence the optimal online direct price, optimal wholesale price, and optimal retail price by substituting relevant parameters into the model, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1a shows that the optimal online selling price increases with the return service level. The effect of reference pricing depends on consumer channel preference. When a larger proportion of consumers prefer the offline channel, a stronger reference price effect increases the online selling price. Conversely, when fewer consumers prefer the offline channel, the online selling price decreases as the reference price effect strengthens. These results illustrate the moderating role of the reference price effect in the relationship between consumer channel preference and online pricing.

Figure 1b indicates that the optimal wholesale price increases with consumer preference for the offline channel, the strength of the reference price effect, and the return service level within the examined parameter region. The wholesale price is more sensitive to changes in the reference price effect than to changes in the return service level in the numerical setting. These results suggest that both consumer price perceptions and return service provision play important roles in determining the manufacturer’s wholesale pricing decisions.

Figure 1c shows that the optimal offline retail price increases with consumer preference for the offline channel, the reference price effect, and the return service level. This indicates that stronger offline channel preference and improved return service provision support higher equilibrium offline retail prices under decentralized decision-making.

Further, within the context of decentralized decision-making, the influence of the reference price effect is investigated and the level of return service on the optimal demand d1d∗, d2d∗ and the corresponding findings are presented in Figure 2.

According to Figure 2a, the stronger consumers’ inclination toward the offline channel, the less the manufacturer’s need for the channel of online sales, and the greater the decline when the reference price impact is small. The reference price impact can help manufacturers moderate profit loss resulting from channel preference. The provision of return service by manufacturers serves a vital function in increasing sales via the online channel.

According to Figure 2b, the more consumers with a preference for offline channels there are, the more the retailer’s demand for such channels rises. As the reference price impact grows, the quantity demand declines; moreover, the reference price impact exerts only a minor influence on the extent of this decline in quantity demand. The reference price impact has a small impact on the retailer’s channel preference. Retailers offering returns promotes increased sales via the online channel.

Finally, the influence of the reference price impact is investigated, and the level of return service on the optimal profit π1d∗, π2d∗, as well as the optimal supply chain profits within the context of decentralized decision-making are analyzed, and the corresponding findings are presented in Figure 3.

Figure 3a shows that the manufacturer’s profit increases with the return service level and the reference price effect within the examined parameter region. The influence of consumer channel preference depends on the strength of the reference price effect. When the reference price effect is relatively weak, a stronger preference for the online channel is associated with higher manufacturer profit. As the reference price effect strengthens, this relationship may reverse, making a greater preference for the offline channel more favorable to the manufacturer.

Figure 3b illustrates the joint effects of the reference price effect and return service level on the retailer’s profit. A higher return service level generally improves retailer profitability in the examined parameter region. When the return service level is sufficiently high, a stronger reference price effect may also increase the retailer’s profit, whereas its effect can be adverse at relatively low service levels. This conditional relationship becomes more pronounced when consumer preference for the offline channel is stronger.

Figure 3c shows that the total supply chain profit under decentralized decision-making increases with the return service level. Within the examined parameter region, a stronger reference price effect also improves total supply chain profit, as the manufacturer’s profit gains can outweigh the retailer’s profit losses when the return service level is relatively low. The magnitude of this effect varies with consumer channel preference.

sec.title: 4.2. Analysis of How Reference Price Effects and Return Services Exert an Impact Within Centralized Decision-Making
sec.p: In the context of centralized decision-making, we examine how the reference price impact b and the level of return service e impact the optimal web-based direct price p1c∗ and the optimal offline retail price p2c∗, and Figure 4 displays the results.

As shown in Figure 4, under the centralized decision-making scenario where the supply chain reaches its optimal state, both the direct online sales price and the offline retail price rise as the return service level improves. In addition, the manufacturer’s direct online price and the retailer’s offline retail price are both affected by the reference price effect and consumer channel preferences. When a substantial proportion of consumers in the market prefer offline channels, the direct online price is lower than the offline channel price, especially as the reference price impact intensifies. The direct online price gradually declines, while the offline retail price increases steadily. This phenomenon stems from the return service level, which to some degree pushes up consumers’ reference prices and weakens the reference price influence’s impact on decision-making of the price. In scenarios where a bigger share of consumers in the market favor online channels, the direct online price is lower than the price of the offline channel. Moreover, as the impact of the reference price grows, both the direct online price and the offline retail price go up little by little. Then, within the centralized decision-making framework, we examine how the reference price impact b and the level of return service e influence the optimal need of the manufacturer and the optimal need of the retailer, with the findings presented in Figure 5.

According to Figure 5, within the context of centralized decision-making, sales offline exceed sales online as a larger share of consumers favor offline channels. However, when the customer reference price impact progressively intensifies, the offline sales of the retailer decline little by little, while the manufacturer’s online sales increase gradually. When a bigger proportion of consumers opt for online channels, offline sales are lower than online sales. In a similar vein, with the gradual intensification of the consumer reference price impact, retailers’ offline sales show a downward trend, whereas manufacturers’ online sales exhibit an upward tendency. Finally, within the centralized decision-making framework, we examine how the reference price impact b and the return service level e influence the supply chain’s optimal profitability, with the findings presented in Figure 6.

According to Figure 6, the total supply chain profit under centralized decision-making increases with the return service level. A stronger preference for the offline channel is also associated with higher total supply chain profit in the numerical setting. Furthermore, the total supply chain profit increases with the reference price effect, and this effect is more pronounced when a larger proportion of consumers prefer the online channel. Figure 6 shows that the total supply chain profit under centralized decision-making increases with the return service level. A stronger preference for the offline channel is also associated with higher total supply chain profit in the numerical setting. Furthermore, the total supply chain profit increases with the reference price effect, and this effect is more pronounced when a larger proportion of consumers prefer the online channel.

sec.title: 4.3. Investigation on How Reference Price Impacts and Return Services Influence Outcomes Across Diverse Decision-Making
sec.p: Based on the above cross-sectional analysis, the influences of the reference price impact and the level of return service regarding the optimal equilibrium outcome under centralized and decentralized decisions, respectively, are derived, while the optimal profits under different decisions are then analyzed vertically for better depth. Within this segment, we investigate the way the reference price impact and return service level influence the supply chain’s optimal profitability in the context of varying decision-making, and then we obtain their results shown in Figure 7, respectively.

According to Figure 7, the supply chain profit under centralized decision-making is higher than the one under decentralized decision-making. Based on the numerical results, the profit difference between the two decision modes narrows as the reference price impact grows, and this difference is larger when v = 0.8 than when v = 0.3. In cases where the share of consumers favoring offline channels is high, the more pronounced the reference price impact is in narrowing the profit differential.
Then, to analyze the value-added profits Δπ, we can obtain the effect of reference price influence and return service level on value-added profits, as Figure 8 presents.

Figure 8 shows that the incremental total supply chain profit from coordination decreases as the reference price effect strengthens for both v = 0.3 and v = 0.8. The coordination gain is larger when v = 0.8, but it also decreases more sharply with the reference price effect. These results indicate that the potential profit improvement from coordination depends on consumer channel preference and reference-price sensitivity.

sec.title: 4.4. Analysis of How Reference Price Impacts and Return Services Influence Outcomes Under Coordination
sec.p: Let D=200,a=0.8, k=23, r = 0.02, u = 0.2, θ = 0.8, c = 0.5, and we examine the impact of the reference price influence and the return service level on prices and value-added profits before and after coordination; their results are shown in Figure 9.

According to Figure 9a,b, an expansion in return service provision is associated with upward adjustments in both the online price of the manufacturer and offline price of the retailer, particularly with a small base of consumers favoring the offline channel. With the intensification of the reference price influence, the coordinated price evolves from being lower to higher than the price set under decentralized decision-making.

As indicated in Figure 9c,d, where the count of consumers favoring online channels is low, the higher the return service level is, the higher both the direct online price of the manufacturer and the offline retail price of the retailer are. Both coordinated online and offline prices are recorded at a discount relative to their decentralized counterparts.

To analyze well the reference price effects and the impact of the level of return service on wholesale price difference and value-added profits of supply chain members, let v = 0.8; we can draw the chart of the effect shown in Figure 10 and Figure 11.

Figure 10 shows that, when consumers have a strong preference for the offline channel, the wholesale price difference between decentralized and coordinated decision-making decreases as the reference price effect strengthens. This indicates that the wholesale price adjustment required for coordination becomes smaller within the examined parameter region. Building upon the above analysis, it can be observed that the reference price impact imposes a more pronounced influence on the supply chain when the proportion of consumers favoring offline channels is higher.

According to Figure 11a, the obvious difference in the manufacturer’s profits after the coordination of the two-part pricing contract and those under decentralized decision-making decreases with the strengthening of the reference price impact, especially when a substantial amount of consumers favors offline channels.

According to Figure 11b, in the context of a substantial amount of consumers favoring offline channels, the difference between the retailer’s profit in the context of decision-making decentralization after the coordination of the two-part pricing contract decreases as the reference price effect increases.

sec.title: 4.5. Verification of the Analytical Results
sec.p: To verify the analytical results, we input the baseline parameters into the closed-form solutions and recompute the equilibrium outcomes at the representative parameter points reported in Table 4. At every point, the first-order conditions are satisfied with residuals smaller than 10−8, all equilibrium prices and demands are positive, and the feasible interval of the fixed transfer fee in (43) and (44) is non-empty. These checks confirm that the closed-form solutions and the coordination contract are implemented correctly in the numerical analysis.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: With respect to the decision-making problem of the dual-channel supply chain, including a dominant manufacturer and a single retailer, we construct a few models discerning the reference price influence and the return service level, and utilize these results to dissect optimal pricing decisions and discuss their impact. Based on the discussion and subsequent analytical findings, key conclusions and corresponding recommendations are outlined below:

(1) In a dual-channel supply chain that accounts for the reference price impact as well as the return service, the introduction of the return service influences not just the reference price but also the online and offline channel needs. The influence of the return service level on the profits of the dual-channel supply chain is positively correlated in the feasible parameter region.

(2) The role of consumer channel preference only affects manufacturers’ online prices differently; under decentralized decision-making, manufacturers’ online prices climb as the reference price effect intensifies among a larger share of offline-preferring consumers, while the trend reverses with a smaller share of such consumers. The results are consistent between centralized and decentralized decision-making.

(3) The manufacturer’s online channel demand and revenue increase with the strengthening of the reference price effect, whereas the retailer’s offline demand and revenue tend to decline in the parameter regions examined. The introduction of return services increases both the wholesale price and offline retail price when consumers have stronger preferences for the offline channel. Moreover, although a stronger reference price effect can reduce the retailer’s revenue when the return service level is relatively low, a sufficiently high service level can offset this adverse effect, resulting in higher overall supply chain profits in the parameter regions examined.

(4) As the reference price effect grows within the admissible parameter region, the income of the manufacturer firm increases, while the retailer’s profit may decrease when the return service level is not sufficiently high. The proposed two-part pricing contract provides a feasible interval of fixed transfer fees within which supply chain coordination can be achieved while ensuring that both the manufacturer and the retailer obtain profits no lower than their decentralized levels. Both the manufacturer and retailer’s returns are larger after coordination than under non-centralized decision-making, and the larger the effect of reference price, the smaller the rise in returns.

This paper examines pricing and coordination decisions for a single product in a manufacturer-led dual-channel supply chain under the reference price effect and return service considerations. Although real-world sales scenarios are more complex—for example, manufacturers may collaborate with multiple retailers across different channels, and retailers may occupy a dominant position—the strategies developed here provide a theoretical reference for pricing and return service decisions in the dual-channel setting.
